title: Εὐρυλόχου βουλή
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Eurylochus answers Odysseus bitterly: Odysseus must be made of iron, the men are worn out, and night winds destroy ships, so they should rest and eat ashore. Odysseus sees that some power is plotting evil and gives way, but first makes every man swear not to harm any herd or flock they find and to eat only the food Circe gave. They moor in a hollow harbour near sweet water, weep for the men Scylla took, and sleep. In the night Zeus sends a squall, and at dawn the ship is dragged into a cave of the nymphs, where Odysseus warns them again against the Sun’s cattle. A month of South and East winds follows; when the food runs out the men fish and hunt, and Odysseus goes inland to pray and is put to sleep. Eurylochus then urges them to sacrifice the best of the cattle, promising a temple at home and saying he would rather drown than waste away on a desert island. They agree, kill the cattle, and make the sacrifice with leaves for barley and water for wine. Odysseus wakes, comes near the ship, smells the burning fat, and cries out to the gods.

sentences.t: σχέτλιός εἰς, Ὀδυσεῦ·
sentences.tr: schetlios eis, Odyseu·
sentences.l: “Cruel you are, Odysseus;
sentences.i: “You are cruel, Odysseus;
sentences.n: Eurylochus is speaking; his speech closes at 294 with ‘So spoke Eurylochus’. εἰς is the epic second person singular of εἰμί (Attic εἶ), ‘you are’, and σχέτλιος is the house word ‘cruel’: a hard word for a man who will not give way to others’ suffering. What Eurylochus means by it is spelled out in the lines that follow, where Odysseus is made of iron and never tires. Ὀδυσεῦ is the vocative of Ὀδυσσεύς.

sentences.t:
περί τοι μένος, οὐδέ τι γυῖα
κάμνεις·
sentences.tr:
peri toi menos, oude ti guia
kamneis·
sentences.l:
exceedingly for you is strength, and not at all in your limbs
do you grow weary;
sentences.i: you have strength beyond measure, and your limbs never tire;
sentences.n: περί is here an adverb, ‘exceedingly’, and τοι is the epic ‘to you’ (σοι), so the Greek says ‘to you there is exceeding strength’, with ἔστι left out. γυῖα, ‘limbs’, is an accusative of respect with κάμνεις, ‘you grow weary’: tired ‘in the limbs’. The ano teleia after κάμνεις ends the clause after the first word of line 280.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥά νυ σοί γε σιδήρεα πάντα τέτυκται,
ὅς ῥ’ ἑτάρους καμάτῳ ἁδηκότας ἠδὲ καὶ ὕπνῳ
οὐκ ἐάᾳς γαίης ἐπιβήμεναι, ἔνθα κεν αὖτε
νήσῳ ἐν ἀμφιρύτῃ λαρὸν τετυκοίμεθα δόρπον,
sentences.tr:
ē rha ny soi ge sidērea panta tetyktai,
hos rh’ hetarous kamatōi hadēkotas ēde kai hypnōi
ouk eaāis gaiēs epibēmenai, entha ken aute
nēsōi en amphirytēi laron tetykoimetha dorpon,
sentences.l:
Truly now for you all things of iron have been made,
you who your companions, worn out by toil and by sleep too,
do not allow on land to set foot, where in turn
on an island flowed-around a tasty supper we might prepare,
sentences.i: Surely you are made all of iron, you who will not let your companions, worn out with toil and with sleep, set foot on land, where we could again prepare ourselves a tasty supper on an island with the sea running all round it,
sentences.n: ἦ ῥά νυ is an emphatic ‘truly, then’, and the perfect passive τέτυκται (τεύχω ‘make’) says everything ‘has been made of iron’. ὅς ῥ’ is ‘you who’, giving the ground of the charge. ἁδηκότας, perfect participle of ἀδέω ‘be sated’, means ‘worn out’ and takes the datives καμάτῳ and ὕπνῳ. ἐάᾳς is ἐᾷς, ‘you allow’, with the vowels opened out; ἐπιβήμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἐπιβαίνω with the genitive γαίης. κεν with the optative τετυκοίμεθα gives ‘where we might prepare’. λαρός ‘tasty’ is a Homeric word whose exact sense is not known. The sentence is cut at this comma, as it would run six lines.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αὔτως διὰ νύκτα θοὴν ἀλάλησθαι ἄνωγας
νήσου ἀποπλαγχθέντας ἐν ἠεροειδέι πόντῳ.
sentences.tr:
all’ autōs dia nykta thoēn alalēsthai anōgas
nēsou apoplanchthentas en ēeroeidei pontōi.
sentences.l:
but just so through the swift night to wander you bid us,
driven-off from the island, in the misty-looking sea.
sentences.i: but you order us to go wandering through the swift night to no purpose, driven off from the island on the misty-looking sea.
sentences.n: θοός ‘swift’ is the word used of ships; of night it presumably means hurrying by, but the sense is not certain. ἀλάλησθαι is a reduplicated perfect infinitive of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’, here simply ‘to be wandering’, after ἄνωγας ‘you bid’, a perfect with present sense. ἀποπλαγχθέντας is the aorist passive participle of ἀποπλάζω ‘drive off course’, in the accusative to agree with an unspoken ‘us’. αὔτως is ‘just so’, that is aimlessly or in vain. ἠεροειδέι πόντῳ is ‘the misty-looking sea’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ νυκτῶν δ’ ἄνεμοι χαλεποί, δηλήματα νηῶν,
γίγνονται·
sentences.tr:
ek nyktōn d’ anemoi chalepoi, dēlēmata nēōn,
gignontai·
sentences.l:
Out of the nights harsh winds, bane of ships,
are born;
sentences.i: Harsh winds, the bane of ships, arise out of the nights;
sentences.n: A general truth about sailing. ἐκ νυκτῶν, ‘out of nights’, means that the winds come up after dark. δηλήματα, ‘things that do harm’, is in apposition to ἄνεμοι ‘winds’, so ‘harsh winds, the bane of ships’; νηῶν is the epic genitive plural (Attic νεῶν). γίγνονται ‘come into being, arise’ is held back to the start of the next line.

sentences.t:
πῇ κέν τις ὑπεκφύγοι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον,
ἤν πως ἐξαπίνης ἔλθῃ ἀνέμοιο θύελλα,
ἢ Νότου ἢ Ζεφύροιο δυσαέος, οἵ τε μάλιστα
νῆα διαρραίουσι θεῶν ἀέκητι ἀνάκτων.
sentences.tr:
pēi ken tis hypekphygoi aipyn olethron,
ēn pōs exapinēs elthēi anemoio thyella,
ē Notou ē Zephyroio dysaeos, hoi te malista
nēa diarraiousi theōn aekēti anaktōn.
sentences.l:
where might one escape steep destruction,
if perhaps suddenly there come of wind a storm-blast,
of the South Wind or of the ill-blowing West Wind, which most of all
shatter the ship against the will of the lord gods?
sentences.i: Where could anyone escape steep destruction, if some storm-blast of wind should suddenly come, from the South Wind or the ill-blowing West Wind, which above all others wreck a ship against the will of the lord gods?
sentences.n: πῇ is ‘where?’, with κεν and the optative ὑπεκφύγοι, ‘could escape’; the question means that there is no escape. ἤν is the epic ἐάν, with the subjunctive ἔλθῃ ‘should come’. ἀνέμοιο θύελλα is ‘a storm-blast of wind’, and the genitives Νότου and Ζεφύροιο (-οιο for -ου) say which winds. δυσαής ‘ill-blowing’ is from δυσ- and ἄημι ‘blow’. οἵ τε is the relative with the epic τε of general truths. διαρραίουσι is ‘smash to pieces’; ἀέκητι ‘against the will of’ takes the genitive θεῶν, with ἀνάκτων ‘lords’ beside it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι νῦν μὲν πειθώμεθα νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ
δόρπον θ’ ὁπλισόμεσθα θοῇ παρὰ νηὶ μένοντες,
ἠῶθεν δ’ ἀναβάντες ἐνήσομεν εὐρέι πόντῳ.
sentences.tr:
all’ ē toi nyn men peithōmetha nykti melainēi
dorpon th’ hoplisomestha thoēi para nēi menontes,
ēōthen d’ anabantes enēsomen eurei pontōi.
sentences.l:
But truly now let us obey black night
and make ready our supper, beside the swift ship staying,
and at dawn, having gone aboard, we will launch her on the wide sea.”
sentences.i: But for now let us give way to dark night and make ready our supper, staying beside the swift ship, and at dawn we will go aboard and launch her on the wide sea.”
sentences.n: ἦ τοι ‘truly’ opens Eurylochus’ practical conclusion; νῦν μέν ‘for now’ is answered by ἠῶθεν δέ ‘but at dawn’. πειθώμεθα and ὁπλισόμεσθα are hortative subjunctives, ‘let us’; ὁπλισόμεσθα is a short-vowel form (-ο-) of the subjunctive, which the epic allows. νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ is the dative of πείθομαι ‘obey, yield to’. ἐνήσομεν comes from ἐνίημι ‘launch’; its object is not written and has to be the ship. The speech ends here, so the English closes the quotation.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Εὐρύλοχος, ἐπὶ δ’ ᾔνεον ἄλλοι ἑταῖροι.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’ Eurylochos, epi d’ ēineon alloi hetairoi.
sentences.l: So spoke Eurylochus, and approved it the other companions.
sentences.i: So spoke Eurylochus, and the rest of his companions agreed.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφατο, elided), a line that closes a speech. ἐπὶ δ’ ᾔνεον is tmesis: the preverb ἐπί stands apart from ᾔνεον, the imperfect of ἐπαινέω ‘approve, assent to’. ἄλλοι ἑταῖροι is ‘the other companions’, all but the speaker. The whole line comes again at 352, with the same English.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε δὴ γίγνωσκον ὃ δὴ κακὰ μήδετο δαίμων,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδων·
sentences.tr:
kai tote dē gignōskon ho dē kaka mēdeto daimōn,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēudōn·
sentences.l:
And then indeed I knew that indeed evils some power was devising,
and speaking to him, winged words I addressed to him:
sentences.i: And then I knew that some power was devising evil, and I spoke to him and addressed him with winged words:
sentences.n: γίγνωσκον is ‘I came to know, I recognised’. ὅ is the neuter relative used as a conjunction, ‘that’, and δαίμων, ‘some power’, is an unnamed divine agent, not a named god; κακά, ‘evils’, is the object of μήδετο ‘was devising’. In 296, μιν is ‘him’, Eurylochus, φωνήσας is the aorist participle of φωνέω ‘speak’, and προσηύδων is the first-person imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘address’; ἔπεα πτερόεντα is the formula ‘winged words’.

sentences.t: Εὐρύλοχ’, ἦ μάλα δή με βιάζετε μοῦνον ἐόντα.
sentences.tr: Euryloch’, ē mala dē me biazete mounon eonta.
sentences.l: “Eurylochus, truly very much now you press me, alone being.
sentences.i: “Eurylochus, you are putting great pressure on me, one man alone.
sentences.n: Odysseus replies. ἦ μάλα δή is ‘truly, very much indeed’. βιάζετε is plural, ‘you (all) force’: he names Eurylochus but addresses the whole crew, who have just agreed with him, and the next line says πάντες ‘all of you’. μοῦνον ἐόντα is ‘being alone’, accusative agreeing with με; ἐόντα is the epic participle of εἰμί (Attic ὄντα). Εὐρύλοχ’ is the vocative Εὐρύλοχε, elided.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν μοι πάντες ὀμόσσατε καρτερὸν ὅρκον·
sentences.tr: all’ age nyn moi pantes omossate karteron horkon·
sentences.l: But come now, to me all swear a mighty oath:
sentences.i: But come now, all of you swear me a solemn oath:
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, introducing a command. ὀμόσσατε is the aorist imperative of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’, with the doubled σσ the epic uses where the metre needs a long syllable; μοι is ‘to me’. καρτερόν is ‘strong, mighty’, and ὅρκος ‘oath’. The colon announces what the oath is to say, which fills the next four lines.

sentences.t:
εἴ κέ τιν’ ἠὲ βοῶν ἀγέλην ἢ πῶυ μέγ’ οἰῶν
εὕρωμεν, μή πού τις ἀτασθαλίῃσι κακῇσιν
ἢ βοῦν ἠέ τι μῆλον ἀποκτάνῃ·
sentences.tr:
ei ke tin’ ēe boōn agelēn ē pōy meg’ oiōn
heurōmen, mē pou tis atasthaliēisi kakēisin
ē boun ēe ti mēlon apoktanēi·
sentences.i: If we find a herd of cattle or a great flock of sheep, let no one in evil, wanton folly kill either an ox or any one of the flock;
sentences.n: The oath’s terms. εἰ with κε and the aorist subjunctive εὕρωμεν is ‘if we should find’, with τιν’ going with ἀγέλην ‘herd’. πῶυ is the neuter noun ‘flock’, with μέγα ‘great’, and οἰῶν is the genitive plural of ὄις ‘sheep’. μή with the aorist subjunctive ἀποκτάνῃ gives ‘let no one kill’, with πού ‘in any way’. ἀτασθαλίῃσι κακῇσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσι (Attic -αις), ‘through evil wanton follies’. μῆλον is one head of small stock, a sheep or goat; the English keeps ‘sheep’ for οἰῶν and says ‘one of the flock’ here.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ ἕκηλοι
ἐσθίετε βρώμην, τὴν ἀθανάτη πόρε Κίρκη.
sentences.tr:
alla hekēloi
esthiete brōmēn, tēn athanatē pore Kirkē.
sentences.l:
but at ease
eat the food that immortal Circe gave.”
sentences.i: but eat at your ease the food that immortal Circe gave us.”
sentences.n: ἀλλά sets the permitted course against the forbidden one. ἕκηλοι ‘at ease, undisturbed’ agrees with the ‘you’ of the imperative ἐσθίετε ‘eat’. βρώμη is ‘food’, and τήν is the relative ‘which’, an article-form used as a pronoun. πόρε is the unaugmented aorist of πόρον ‘gave’ (Attic ἔδωκε). ἀθανάτη, ‘immortal’, describes Circe, a goddess. The speech ends here, so the English closes the quotation.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, οἱ δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀπώμνυον, ὡς ἐκέλευον.
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, hoi d’ autik’ apōmnyon, hōs ekeleuon.
sentences.l: So I spoke, and they at once swore it, as I bade.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and they swore at once, as I had told them to.
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’, the first-person counterpart of ὣς ἔφατο. οἱ is ‘they’, a pronoun, not the article. ἀπώμνυον is the imperfect of ἀπόμνυμι ‘swear solemnly’, here ‘swear the oath’. ἐκέλευον is the first-person imperfect of κελεύω ‘bid’: ‘as I bade’. The men give no speech; their answer is the oath itself.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ὄμοσάν τε τελεύτησάν τε τὸν ὅρκον,
στήσαμεν ἐν λιμένι γλαφυρῷ ἐυεργέα νῆα
ἄγχ’ ὕδατος γλυκεροῖο, καὶ ἐξαπέβησαν ἑταῖροι
νηός, ἔπειτα δὲ δόρπον ἐπισταμένως τετύκοντο.
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ omosan te teleutēsan te ton horkon,
stēsamen en limeni glaphyrōi eyergea nēa
anch’ hydatos glykeroio, kai exapebēsan hetairoi
nēos, epeita de dorpon epistamenōs tetykonto.
sentences.l:
But when then they had sworn and completed the oath,
we moored in a hollow harbour the well-made ship
near sweet water, and disembarked the companions
from the ship, and then supper skilfully they prepared.
sentences.i: When they had sworn and completed the oath, we moored the well-made ship in a hollow harbour near sweet water, and my companions stepped out of the ship and then skilfully prepared a supper.
sentences.n: ὄμοσάν and τελεύτησάν are aorists in -αν without augment (Attic ὤμοσαν, ἐτελεύτησαν): ‘they swore’, ‘they brought to an end’. στήσαμεν is ‘we moored’, literally ‘we made stand’, with νῆα ‘ship’ as object and ἐυεργέα, the house ‘well-made’. γλαφυρῷ is ‘hollow’, and ἄγχ’ ὕδατος γλυκεροῖο is ‘near sweet water’. ἐξαπέβησαν is ‘they stepped off’, with the genitive νηός ‘from the ship’. ἐπισταμένως ‘skilfully’ is the participle of ἐπίσταμαι used as an adverb. τετύκοντο is an epic aorist of τεύχω, ‘they prepared’. The sentence is four lines long and stays whole.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
μνησάμενοι δὴ ἔπειτα φίλους ἔκλαιον ἑταίρους,
οὓς ἔφαγε Σκύλλη γλαφυρῆς ἐκ νηὸς ἑλοῦσα·
sentences.tr:
autar epei posios kai edētyos ex eron hento,
mnēsamenoi dē epeita philous eklaion hetairous,
hous ephage Skyllē glaphyrēs ek nēos helousa·
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, they remembered, and wept for their dear companions, whom Scylla had seized from the hollow ship and eaten;
sentences.n: The first line is a stock line for the end of a meal: ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο, tmesis for ‘they sent out desire’, i.e. put it away, with ἔρον ‘desire’ and the genitives πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ‘of drink and of food’; ἕντο is the aorist middle of ἵημι. μνησάμενοι is the aorist middle participle ‘having remembered’, and ἔκλαιον ‘they wept for’ takes the accusative ἑταίρους. οὓς ἔφαγε is ‘whom she ate’, ἔφαγε being an aorist of ἐσθίω; ἑλοῦσα, ‘having seized’, is the feminine aorist participle of αἱρέω, agreeing with Σκύλλη.

sentences.t: κλαιόντεσσι δὲ τοῖσιν ἐπήλυθε νήδυμος ὕπνος.
sentences.tr: klaiontessi de toisin epēlythe nēdymos hypnos.
sentences.l: And upon them, weeping, came sweet sleep.
sentences.i: And as they wept, sweet sleep came upon them.
sentences.n: κλαιόντεσσι is a dative plural participle in -εσσι, agreeing with τοῖσιν ‘to them’ (a pronoun here, not the article), and both are datives after ἐπήλυθε, the aorist of ἐπέρχομαι ‘come upon’. νήδυμος is a Homeric epithet of sleep; ‘sweet’ is the traditional rendering, but the meaning and origin of the word are not known.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δὲ τρίχα νυκτὸς ἔην, μετὰ δ’ ἄστρα βεβήκει,
ὦρσεν ἔπι ζαῆν ἄνεμον νεφεληγερέτα Ζεὺς
λαίλαπι θεσπεσίῃ, σὺν δὲ νεφέεσσι κάλυψε
γαῖαν ὁμοῦ καὶ πόντον·
sentences.tr:
ēmos de tricha nyktos eēn, meta d’ astra bebēkei,
ōrsen epi zaēn anemon nephelēgereta Zeus
lailapi thespesiēi, syn de nepheessi kalypse
gaian homou kai ponton·
sentences.l:
And when it was in three parts of night, and the stars had moved on,
stirred up a hard-blowing wind cloud-gatherer Zeus
with a wondrous squall, and with clouds he covered
earth and open-sea together;
sentences.i: And when the night was divided in three and the stars had moved on, Zeus who gathers the clouds stirred up a hard-blowing wind in a wondrous squall, and with clouds hid land and sea alike;
sentences.n: ἦμος δέ is ‘and when’. τρίχα ‘in three parts’, with νυκτὸς ἔην, says only that the night stood divided in three; which point of the night is meant is not certain. μετὰ ... βεβήκει is a pluperfect, ‘had gone on’, with μετά as an adverb. ὦρσεν ἔπι is tmesis for ἐπῶρσεν, ‘stirred up’, from ὄρνυμι, and ζαῆν is ‘hard-blowing’ (ζα- is intensive; ἄημι is ‘blow’). λαίλαπι θεσπεσίῃ is ‘with a wondrous squall’. The sentence is cut at the ano teleia in line 315.

sentences.t: ὀρώρει δ’ οὐρανόθεν νύξ.
sentences.tr: orōrei d’ ouranothen nyx.
sentences.l: and night had sprung up from the sky.
sentences.i: and night had sprung up out of the sky.
sentences.n: ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse; (intransitive) arise, spring up’: night ‘had sprung up’. The suffix -θεν marks ‘from’, so οὐρανόθεν is ‘from the sky’. This is the second half of the sentence that the ano teleia divided, and it says that night itself came from above, the clouds shutting out the light.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
νῆα μὲν ὡρμίσαμεν κοῖλον σπέος εἰσερύσαντες.
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
nēa men hōrmisamen koilon speos eiserysantes.
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
the ship we moored, into a hollow cave having dragged it.
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, we moored the ship, having dragged her into a hollow cave.
sentences.n: The dawn formula: ἠριγένεια ‘early-born’ and ῥοδοδάκτυλος ‘rose-fingered’ both go with Ἠώς ‘Dawn’, and φάνη is the aorist passive of φαίνω ‘appeared’. ὡρμίσαμεν is ‘we brought to anchor, moored’; here the ship is hauled out of the water into a cave. εἰσερύσαντες is the aorist participle of εἰσερύω ‘draw in’, and κοῖλον σπέος, ‘a hollow cave’, is the place into which, in the accusative with no preposition.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἔσαν νυμφέων καλοὶ χοροὶ ἠδὲ θόωκοι·
sentences.tr: entha d’ esan nympheōn kaloi choroi ēde thoōkoi·
sentences.l: And there were of nymphs fine dancing-places and seats;
sentences.i: And there the nymphs had fine dancing-places and seats;
sentences.n: ἔσαν is the epic third-person plural imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦσαν). νυμφέων is the genitive plural of νύμφη ‘nymph’, with -έων for Attic -ῶν. χοροί are places for dancing, and θόωκοι is a poetic word for ‘seats’. The cave they have chosen is a haunt of nymphs.

sentences.t: καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἀγορὴν θέμενος μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπον·
sentences.tr: kai tot’ egōn agorēn themenos meta mython eeipon·
sentences.l: and then I, an assembly having set, among them a speech I spoke:
sentences.i: and then I called an assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ. ἀγορὴν θέμενος, ‘having set an assembly’, means ‘having called an assembly’; θέμενος is the aorist middle participle of τίθημι. μετά is an adverb, ‘among them’, and μῦθον ἔειπον is ‘I spoke a speech’, with ἔειπον the aorist with a doubled ε (Attic εἶπον). The colon announces the speech that follows.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, ἐν γὰρ νηὶ θοῇ βρῶσίς τε πόσις τε
ἔστιν, τῶν δὲ βοῶν ἀπεχώμεθα, μή τι πάθωμεν·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi, en gar nēi thoēi brōsis te posis te
estin, tōn de boōn apechōmetha, mē ti pathōmen·
sentences.l:
“O friends, for in the swift ship food and drink
there is, but from the cattle let us keep away, lest we suffer anything;
sentences.i: “Friends, since there is food and drink in the swift ship, let us keep away from the cattle, lest we come to any harm;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks to the whole crew. ὦ φίλοι is ‘O friends’. ἔστιν with the accent on its first syllable is ‘there is’, a singular verb with the double subject βρῶσίς τε πόσις τε ‘food and drink’. τῶν βοῶν, ‘those cattle’, is the genitive after ἀπεχώμεθα ‘let us keep away from’, a subjunctive of exhortation. μή with the aorist subjunctive πάθωμεν is a fear clause, ‘lest we suffer’, with τι ‘anything’ as its object.

sentences.t:
δεινοῦ γὰρ θεοῦ αἵδε βόες καὶ ἴφια μῆλα,
Ἠελίου, ὃς πάντ’ ἐφορᾷ καὶ πάντ’ ἐπακούει.
sentences.tr:
deinou gar theou haide boes kai iphia mēla,
Ēeliou, hos pant’ ephorāi kai pant’ epakouei.
sentences.l:
for of a dread god these cattle and stout flocks are,
of the Sun, who oversees all things and listens to all things.”
sentences.i: for these cattle and stout flocks belong to a dread god, the Sun, who sees everything and hears everything.”
sentences.n: δεινοῦ θεοῦ is a genitive of possession, ‘belonging to a dread god’, with Ἠελίου ‘of the Sun’ (Attic Ἡλίου) naming him in apposition. αἵδε is ‘these here’, feminine plural, for βόες. ἴφια μῆλα is ‘stout flocks’. ἐφορᾷ, from ἐφοράω ‘oversee, look upon’, and ἐπακούει ‘listens to, hears’ are both present tense, each with πάντ’ ‘all things’. The speech ends here, so the English closes the quotation.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπεπείθετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, toisin d’ epepeitheto thymos agēnōr.
sentences.l: So I spoke, and in them their manly spirit was persuaded.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and their proud spirits were won over.
sentences.n: The line says that the speech has worked. τοῖσιν is ‘in them’, a dative, with θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ ‘manly spirit’ (the house ‘proud’ in English); the singular θυμός stands for the spirit of each man. ἐπεπείθετο is the imperfect of ἐπιπείθομαι ‘be persuaded, obey’, with the augment placed after the preverb.

sentences.t:
μῆνα δὲ πάντ’ ἄλληκτος ἄη Νότος, οὐδέ τις ἄλλος
γίγνετ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀνέμων εἰ μὴ Εὖρός τε Νότος τε.
sentences.tr:
mēna de pant’ allēktos aē Notos, oude tis allos
gignet’ epeit’ anemōn ei mē Euros te Notos te.
sentences.l:
And for a month, all of it, unceasing blew the South Wind, nor any other
arose then of winds, except the East Wind and the South Wind.
sentences.i: But for a whole month the South Wind blew without ceasing, and no other wind arose after that except the East Wind and the South Wind.
sentences.n: μῆνα is an accusative of duration, ‘for a month’, and πάντ’ (πάντα) agrees with it, ‘the whole month’. ἄλληκτος is ‘unceasing’. ἄη is the imperfect of ἄημι ‘blow’. ἀνέμων is a partitive genitive, ‘of winds’, and γίγνετ’ (γίγνετο) ‘arose’ is the imperfect of γίγνομαι. Νότος is the South Wind and Εὖρος the East Wind; the Greek names only these two winds.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἧος μὲν σῖτον ἔχον καὶ οἶνον ἐρυθρόν,
τόφρα βοῶν ἀπέχοντο λιλαιόμενοι βιότοιο.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hēos men siton echon kai oinon erythron,
tophra boōn apechonto lilaiomenoi biotoio.
sentences.l:
And they, so long as food they had and wine, red,
for that time from the cattle held off, longing for life.
sentences.i: As long as they had food and red wine, they kept away from the cattle for that time, longing for life.
sentences.n: ἧος μέν is the epic form of εἷος, ‘so long as’, and τόφρα ‘for that time’ is its correlative: ‘as long as ... for that long’. ἔχον is the unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω, ‘they had’. οἶνον ἐρυθρόν is ‘red wine’. ἀπέχοντο, imperfect middle of ἀπέχω, takes the genitive βοῶν, ‘kept themselves away from the cattle’. λιλαιόμενοι, ‘longing for’, takes the genitive βιότοιο, from βίοτος ‘life’; the participle gives their reason for abstaining.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ νηὸς ἐξέφθιτο ἤια πάντα,
καὶ δὴ ἄγρην ἐφέπεσκον ἀλητεύοντες ἀνάγκῃ,
ἰχθῦς ὄρνιθάς τε, φίλας ὅ τι χεῖρας ἵκοιτο,
γναμπτοῖς ἀγκίστροισιν, ἔτειρε δὲ γαστέρα λιμός·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē nēos exephthito ēia panta,
kai dē agrēn ephepeskon alēteuontes anankēi,
ichthys ornithas te, philas ho ti cheiras hikoito,
gnamptois ankistroisin, eteire de gastera limos·
sentences.l:
But when indeed from the ship were used up the provisions, all,
then indeed game they went after, wandering by necessity,
fish and birds, whatever to their dear hands might come,
with bent hooks, and hunger wore away their bellies;
sentences.i: But when all the provisions from the ship were used up, they went after game, roaming of necessity, fish and birds, whatever came to their hands, with bent hooks, while hunger wore away at their bellies;
sentences.n: ἐξέφθιτο is an aorist middle of ἐκφθίνω ‘waste away, be used up’; its subject is the neuter plural ἤια ‘provisions’, which takes a singular verb, and νηός is ‘from the ship’. ἐφέπεσκον is an iterative imperfect in -σκ-, ‘they would go after’, with ἄγρην ‘game, catch’; ἀνάγκῃ is ‘by necessity’. In 331, ὅ τι is ‘whatever’, with the optative ἵκοιτο ‘might come’ of repeated action; φίλας ‘dear’ is the Homeric way of saying ‘their own’. γναμπτοῖς ἀγκίστροισιν is ‘with bent hooks’. γαστέρα is a singular ‘belly’ standing for the bellies of all, and the English says ‘bellies’.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἀνὰ νῆσον ἀπέστιχον, ὄφρα θεοῖσιν
εὐξαίμην, εἴ τίς μοι ὁδὸν φήνειε νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
dē tot’ egōn ana nēson apestichon, ophra theoisin
euxaimēn, ei tis moi hodon phēneie neesthai.
sentences.l:
Then indeed I up through the island went away, so that to the gods
I might pray, if any would for me a way show to go home.
sentences.i: Then I went off up through the island, so that I might pray to the gods, in case any of them would show me a way to get home.
sentences.n: ἀνὰ νῆσον is ‘up through the island’, and ἀπέστιχον is the first-person imperfect of ἀποστείχω ‘go off’. ὄφρα with the optative εὐξαίμην gives purpose, ‘so that I might pray’; εὔχομαι with a dative is ‘pray to’. εἴ τις ... φήνειε, from φαίνω ‘show’, is ‘if any (god) would show’, with the optative φήνειε keeping the hope open, and νέεσθαι is the epic infinitive of νέομαι ‘go, return home’: ‘a way to return’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ διὰ νήσου ἰὼν ἤλυξα ἑταίρους,
χεῖρας νιψάμενος, ὅθ’ ἐπὶ σκέπας ἦν ἀνέμοιο,
ἠρώμην πάντεσσι θεοῖς οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē dia nēsou iōn ēlyxa hetairous,
cheiras nipsamenos, hoth’ epi skepas ēn anemoio,
ērōmēn pantessi theois hoi Olympon echousin·
sentences.i: But when I had gone through the island and slipped away from my companions, I washed my hands in a spot sheltered from the wind and prayed to all the gods who hold Olympus;
sentences.n: ἤλυξα is the aorist of ἀλύσκω ‘escape, evade’, here with the accusative ἑταίρους: ‘I got away from my companions’. νιψάμενος is the aorist middle participle of νίζω ‘wash’, with χεῖρας ‘my hands’; he washes, then prays. ὅθ’ is ὅθι ‘where’, and ἐπὶ ... ἦν is tmesis for ἐπῆν, ‘there was’ (ἔπειμι); σκέπας is ‘shelter’, with the genitive ἀνέμοιο ‘from the wind’. ἠρώμην is the first-person imperfect middle of ἀράομαι ‘pray’, with the dative θεοῖς. οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν is ‘who hold Olympus’.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἄρα μοι γλυκὺν ὕπνον ἐπὶ βλεφάροισιν ἔχευαν.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ara moi glykyn hypnon epi blepharoisin echeuan.
sentences.l: and they then for me sweet sleep upon my eyelids poured.
sentences.i: and they poured sweet sleep over my eyelids.
sentences.n: οἱ is ‘they’, the gods of the line before, a pronoun and not the article. μοι is the dative ‘for me, on me’. ἔχευαν is the epic aorist of χέω ‘pour’, in -αν, and βλεφάροισιν is the dative plural of βλέφαρον ‘eyelid’, after ἐπί ‘upon’. γλυκύν is ‘sweet’, the same English as νήδυμος at 311, though the Greek word is a different one. His prayer in 334 asked for a way home; what comes is sleep.

sentences.t: Εὐρύλοχος δ’ ἑτάροισι κακῆς ἐξήρχετο βουλῆς·
sentences.tr: Eurylochos d’ hetaroisi kakēs exērcheto boulēs·
sentences.l: And Eurylochus to his companions of an evil counsel began:
sentences.i: And Eurylochus began to give his companions evil counsel:
sentences.n: ἐξήρχετο is the imperfect of ἐξάρχομαι ‘begin, lead off’, which takes a genitive of the thing begun: κακῆς βουλῆς, ‘an evil counsel’. ἑτάροισι is the dative plural of the short form ἕταρος, beside ἑταῖρος. While Odysseus sleeps, Eurylochus makes his proposal; the colon announces it.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ μύθων κακά περ πάσχοντες ἑταῖροι.
πάντες μὲν στυγεροὶ θάνατοι δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσι,
λιμῷ δ’ οἴκτιστον θανέειν καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖν.
sentences.tr:
keklyte meu mythōn kaka per paschontes hetairoi.
pantes men stygeroi thanatoi deiloisi brotoisi,
limōi d’ oiktiston thaneein kai potmon epispein.
sentences.l:
“Hear my words, evils though suffering, companions.
All deaths are hateful to miserable mortals,
but by hunger most lamentable to die and meet one’s doom.
sentences.i: “Hear my words, companions, suffering woes as you are. Every death is hateful to miserable mortals, but to die of hunger and meet that doom is the most lamentable of all.
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, with μευ the epic genitive ‘my’ (μου) on μύθων ‘words’. κακά περ πάσχοντες is ‘though suffering evils’, with περ giving the concession. πάντες ... θάνατοι is ‘all deaths’, στυγεροί ‘hateful’, δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσι ‘for miserable mortals’. In 342 οἴκτιστον is the superlative of οἰκτρός ‘lamentable’, with ἐστί understood; θανέειν and ἐπισπεῖν are aorist infinitives, ‘to die’ and ‘to meet (one’s doom)’. The first sentence is a single line, and the three lines make one unit.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’, Ἠελίοιο βοῶν ἐλάσαντες ἀρίστας
ῥέξομεν ἀθανάτοισι, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν.
sentences.tr:
all’ aget’, Ēelioio boōn elasantes aristas
rhexomen athanatoisi, toi ouranon euryn echousin.
sentences.l:
But come, of the Sun’s cattle having driven off the best,
let us sacrifice to the immortals, who the wide sky hold.
sentences.i: But come, let us drive off the best of the Sun’s cattle and sacrifice them to the immortals who hold the wide sky.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ is ‘but come’, the plural of ἄγε. ἐλάσαντες is the aorist participle of ἐλαύνω ‘drive off’, and ἀρίστας, accusative feminine plural, is ‘the best ones’, with Ἠελίοιο βοῶν the genitives ‘of the cattle of the Sun’. ῥέξομεν is a short-vowel aorist subjunctive of ῥέζω ‘do’, which also means ‘perform a sacrifice’: ‘let us sacrifice’, with the cattle understood. τοί is here the relative ‘who’, the old demonstrative used as one, and οὐρανὸν εὐρύν is ‘the wide sky’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν εἰς Ἰθάκην ἀφικοίμεθα, πατρίδα γαῖαν,
αἶψά κεν Ἠελίῳ Ὑπερίονι πίονα νηὸν
τεύξομεν, ἐν δέ κε θεῖμεν ἀγάλματα πολλὰ καὶ ἐσθλά.
sentences.tr:
ei de ken eis Ithakēn aphikoimetha, patrida gaian,
aipsa ken Ēeliōi Hyperioni piona nēon
teuxomen, en de ke theimen agalmata polla kai esthla.
sentences.l:
But if to Ithaca we should come, the fatherland,
at once for the Sun Hyperion a rich temple
we will build, and in it we would set ornaments, many and good.
sentences.i: And if we ever reach Ithaca, our fatherland, we shall at once build a rich temple for the Sun, Hyperion, and set many good ornaments in it.
sentences.n: εἰ with κε and the optative ἀφικοίμεθα is ‘if we should reach’, and πατρίδα γαῖαν, ‘fatherland’, is in apposition to Ἰθάκην. τεύξομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive (or a future) of τεύχω ‘make, build’; κε with θεῖμεν, the epic aorist optative of τίθημι, gives ‘we would set up’. Ἠελίῳ Ὑπερίονι is ‘for the Sun, Hyperion’, Hyperion being a name of the Sun. νηόν is the accusative of νηός ‘temple’ (Attic νεώς), not the ‘ship’ word; πίονα ‘fat’ is ‘rich’ of a temple. ἀγάλματα, from ἀγάλλομαι ‘delight’, are things that give pleasure, here ornaments set up as offerings.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ χολωσάμενός τι βοῶν ὀρθοκραιράων
νῆ’ ἐθέλῃ ὀλέσαι, ἐπὶ δ’ ἕσπωνται θεοὶ ἄλλοι,
βούλομ’ ἅπαξ πρὸς κῦμα χανὼν ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὀλέσσαι,
ἢ δηθὰ στρεύγεσθαι ἐὼν ἐν νήσῳ ἐρήμῃ.
sentences.tr:
ei de cholōsamenos ti boōn orthokrairaōn
nē’ ethelēi olesai, epi d’ hespōntai theoi alloi,
boulom’ hapax pros kyma chanōn apo thymon olessai,
ē dētha streugesthai eōn en nēsōi erēmēi.
sentences.l:
But if, angered somewhat over the straight-horned cattle,
the ship he is willing to destroy, and follow him the other gods,
I prefer once, toward a wave gaping, my spirit to lose
rather than long to be worn away, being on a desert island.”
sentences.i: But if he is angry over his straight-horned cattle and means to destroy our ship, and the other gods follow him, I would rather lose my life once, with my mouth open to a wave, than be slowly worn away on a desert island.”
sentences.n: χολωσάμενος, the aorist middle participle of χολόω ‘anger’, takes the genitive βοῶν ὀρθοκραιράων, ‘over the straight-horned cattle’ (the second part of ὀρθοκραίρων is related to κέρας ‘horn’); τι is adverbial, ‘somewhat’. εἰ ... ἐθέλῃ is the epic subjunctive without κε, ‘if he is willing’, and ἐπὶ δ’ ἕσπωνται is tmesis for ‘and others follow’, from ἐφέπομαι. βούλομαι is ‘I prefer’ and ἅπαξ ‘once for all’; χανών is the aorist participle of χάσκω ‘gape’; ἀπὸ ... ὀλέσσαι is tmesis for ‘lose’, with θυμός here the life that leaves a man. The speech ends here, so the English closes the quotation.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Εὐρύλοχος, ἐπὶ δ’ ᾔνεον ἄλλοι ἑταῖροι.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’ Eurylochos, epi d’ ēineon alloi hetairoi.
sentences.l: So spoke Eurylochus, and approved it the other companions.
sentences.i: So spoke Eurylochus, and the rest of his companions agreed.
sentences.n: The same line as 294, with the same English: ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο, and ᾔνεον is the imperfect of ἐπαινέω, split from its preverb ἐπί by tmesis. At 294 the men agreed to Eurylochus’ proposal to stay ashore for the night; here they agree to his proposal to take the cattle, which is what they swore not to do (298–302).

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ Ἠελίοιο βοῶν ἐλάσαντες ἀρίστας
ἐγγύθεν, οὐ γὰρ τῆλε νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
βοσκέσκονθ’ ἕλικες καλαὶ βόες εὐρυμέτωποι·
sentences.tr:
autika d’ Ēelioio boōn elasantes aristas
engythen, ou gar tēle neos kyanoprōiroio
boskeskonth’ helikes kalai boes eurymetōpoi·
sentences.i: At once they drove off the best of the Sun’s cattle from close by, for not far from the dark-prowed ship the fine cattle of crumpled horn and broad brow were grazing;
sentences.n: ἐλάσαντες is ‘having driven off’, as at 343, with the same object ἀρίστας ‘the best ones’. ἐγγύθεν is ‘from near by’, with -θεν ‘from’. βοσκέσκονθ’ is βοσκέσκοντο, an iterative imperfect in -σκ- of βόσκω ‘graze’; the θ comes from the rough breathing of the next word. νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο is ‘of the dark-prowed ship’. ἕλικες is a word for ‘twisting, curving’, so ‘crumple-horned’; εὐρυμέτωποι is ‘broad-browed’, and καλαί ‘fine’.

sentences.t:
τὰς δὲ περίστησάν τε καὶ εὐχετόωντο θεοῖσιν,
φύλλα δρεψάμενοι τέρενα δρυὸς ὑψικόμοιο·
sentences.tr:
tas de peristēsan te kai euchetoōnto theoisin,
phylla drepsamenoi terena dryos hypsikomoio·
sentences.l:
and these they stood around and prayed to the gods,
having plucked tender leaves from a high-crowned oak;
sentences.i: They stood around them and prayed to the gods, having plucked tender leaves from a high-crowned oak;
sentences.n: τάς is ‘them’, the cattle: the article-form is a pronoun here. περίστησαν is the unaugmented aorist of περιΐστημι in its intransitive sense, ‘they stood around’. εὐχετόωντο is the imperfect of εὐχετάομαι, a lengthened form of εὔχομαι ‘pray’, with the dative θεοῖσιν. δρεψάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of δρέπω ‘pluck’; τέρενα is the neuter plural of τέρην ‘tender’; δρυός is the genitive of δρῦς ‘oak’ and ὑψικόμοιο (-οιο for -ου) ‘high-crowned’. The next line says why leaves.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἔχον κρῖ λευκὸν ἐυσσέλμου ἐπὶ νηός.
sentences.tr: ou gar echon kri leukon eysselmou epi nēos.
sentences.l: for they had not white barley on the well-benched ship.
sentences.i: for they had no white barley on their well-benched ship.
sentences.n: γάρ explains the leaves: the men have no barley, and the oak leaves stand in for it. κρῖ is a short form meaning ‘barley’, found only in the nominative and accusative, and λευκόν is ‘white’. ἔχον is the unaugmented imperfect ‘they had’. ἐυσσέλμου, ‘well-benched’, is built on σέλμα ‘a ship’s bench’, and ἐπὶ νηός, with the genitive, is ‘on the ship’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ εὔξαντο καὶ ἔσφαξαν καὶ ἔδειραν,
μηρούς τ’ ἐξέταμον κατά τε κνίσῃ ἐκάλυψαν
δίπτυχα ποιήσαντες, ἐπ’ αὐτῶν δ’ ὠμοθέτησαν.
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ euxanto kai esphaxan kai edeiran,
mērous t’ exetamon kata te knisēi ekalypsan
diptycha poiēsantes, ep’ autōn d’ ōmothetēsan.
sentences.l:
But when then they had prayed and slaughtered and flayed,
the thighs they cut out and covered them over with fat,
making it double-folded, and on them they laid raw pieces.
sentences.i: But when they had prayed, slaughtered the beasts and flayed them, they cut out the thighs, covered them with fat folded double, and laid raw morsels on them.
sentences.n: The sacrifice, in stock lines. εὔξαντο is the aorist middle of εὔχομαι ‘pray’, ἔσφαξαν the aorist of σφάζω ‘cut the throat, slaughter’, ἔδειραν of δέρω ‘flay’. μηρούς are the thighs, the part burnt for the gods (see 364); ἐξέταμον is the aorist of ἐκτάμνω ‘cut out’. κατά ... ἐκάλυψαν is tmesis for ‘covered over’, with κνίσῃ ‘with fat’; δίπτυχα is ‘double-folded’, and ἐπ’ αὐτῶν ... ὠμοθέτησαν is ‘they laid raw pieces on them’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εἶχον μέθυ λεῖψαι ἐπ’ αἰθομένοις ἱεροῖσιν,
ἀλλ’ ὕδατι σπένδοντες ἐπώπτων ἔγκατα πάντα.
sentences.tr:
oud’ eichon methy leipsai ep’ aithomenois hieroisin,
all’ hydati spendontes epōptōn enkata panta.
sentences.l:
Nor had they wine to pour on the burning sacrifices,
but pouring libation with water they roasted all the entrails.
sentences.i: They had no wine to pour over the burning sacrifices, so they made their libation with water and roasted all the entrails.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ εἶχον is ‘nor did they have’, εἶχον being the augmented imperfect of ἔχω. μέθυ is ‘wine’, an old neuter noun, and λεῖψαι is the aorist infinitive of λείβω ‘pour’. αἰθομένοις, from αἴθω ‘burn’, agrees with ἱεροῖσιν ‘sacrifices’. ὕδατι is a dative of means, ‘with water’, with σπένδοντες ‘pouring libations’. ἐπώπτων is the imperfect of ἐποπτάω ‘roast’, and ἔγκατα are the entrails. Wine would have been poured on the burning offering; water has to do.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατὰ μῆρ’ ἐκάη καὶ σπλάγχνα πάσαντο,
μίστυλλόν τ’ ἄρα τἆλλα καὶ ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ἔπειραν.
sentences.tr:
autar epei kata mēr’ ekaē kai splanchna pasanto,
mistyllon t’ ara talla kai amph’ obeloisin epeiran.
sentences.l:
But when the thigh-pieces were burned up and they had tasted the entrails,
they cut up the rest then into pieces and pierced them around spits.
sentences.i: But when the thigh-pieces were burned up and they had tasted the entrails, they cut up the rest into small pieces and pierced them on spits.
sentences.n: κατὰ μῆρ’ ἐκάη is tmesis for κατεκάη, ‘were burned down’, with the neuter plural μῆρα ‘thigh-pieces’ taking a singular verb. πάσαντο is the aorist middle of πατέομαι ‘taste, eat of’. In 365, μίστυλλον is the imperfect of μιστύλλω ‘cut into small pieces’, τἆλλα is τὰ ἄλλα ‘the rest’ with crasis, and ἀμφ’ ὀβελοῖσιν ἔπειραν is ‘they pierced (them) on spits’, from πείρω ‘pierce’, with ἀμφί ‘around’.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε μοι βλεφάρων ἐξέσσυτο νήδυμος ὕπνος,
βῆν δ’ ἰέναι ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν καὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
kai tote moi blepharōn exessyto nēdymos hypnos,
bēn d’ ienai epi nēa thoēn kai thina thalassēs.
sentences.l:
And then from my eyelids rushed out sweet sleep,
and I set out to go to the swift ship and the shore of the sea.
sentences.i: And then sweet sleep rushed out of my eyelids, and I set out for the swift ship and the shore of the sea.
sentences.n: μοι is the dative of the person affected, ‘my’, with βλεφάρων ‘from my eyelids’, a genitive of separation: the sleep that was poured on them at 338 now leaves. ἐξέσσυτο is the aorist middle of ἐκσεύω ‘rush out’, the doubled σ being epic. βῆν is the first-person aorist (Attic ἔβην), with the infinitive ἰέναι, ‘I set out to go’; νῆα θοήν is ‘the swift ship’, and θῖνα ‘shore, beach’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦα κιὼν νεὸς ἀμφιελίσσης,
καὶ τότε με κνίσης ἀμφήλυθεν ἡδὺς ἀυτμή.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē schedon ēa kiōn neos amphielissēs,
kai tote me knisēs amphēlythen hēdys aytmē.
sentences.l:
But when indeed near I was going to the both-sides-curving ship,
then around me came of the fat a sweet vapour.
sentences.i: But when I was drawing near the ship, curved on both sides, then the sweet smell of the fat came about me.
sentences.n: σχεδόν is ‘near’; ἦα is an imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’ and κιών the participle of κίω ‘go’, together ‘I was going’. νεὸς ἀμφιελίσσης is ‘of the ship curved on both sides’; the sense of ἀμφιέλισσα is disputed, and ‘rowed on both sides’ is also guessed. κνίσης is the genitive of κνίση, the fat and its savour. ἀυτμή is ‘breath, vapour’, and ἡδύς ‘sweet’ stands with it here in its masculine form. ἀμφήλυθεν is the aorist of ἀμφέρχομαι ‘come around’.

sentences.t: οἰμώξας δὲ θεοῖσι μέγ’ ἀθανάτοισι γεγώνευν·
sentences.tr: oimōxas de theoisi meg’ athanatoisi gegōneun·
sentences.l: And groaning, to the gods loudly, the immortals, I cried out:
sentences.i: And groaning, I cried out loudly to the immortal gods:
sentences.n: οἰμώξας is the aorist participle of οἰμώζω ‘groan, wail aloud’. μέγ’ (μέγα) is an adverb, ‘loudly, greatly’, and goes with the verb, not with ἀθανάτοισι; θεοῖσι ... ἀθανάτοισι is ‘to the immortal gods’. γεγώνευν is an imperfect of the verb for calling out so as to be heard at a distance, here first person singular. The colon announces the cry itself, which lies beyond this part.
